judgement.reason: It says no bishop forces another, which bears on who settles disputes but does not say who did settle them.
It shows God moving the heart through the Spirit, but it argues where love of God comes from and is not a description of God's character.
It says the newborn has no sins of his own but took the contagion of death, which bears on the question, yet it never speaks of guilt and is about not delaying baptism.
It shows how two sources differ and the difference is left open, but it does not say how much of the community's claims survive scrutiny.
It shows scripture speaking to a hearer who fears to repent, but it does not answer what a confused or bored reader is missing.
It puts Scripture above bishops' letters and councils while allowing that bishops and councils carry authority that can be corrected.
It shows a crowd following Cyprian openly at his sentence and says nothing on whether believers hid underground.
It shows how a bishop's authority was established, by God's judgment and the people's favour, though only in Cyprian's case.
It speaks of the motive and duty of those who feed Christ's flock, not of how authority was established, and names no rank.
It shows one response to the failed, a provision for sick penitents holding martyrs' letters, not the church's general response.
It shows infant baptism already practised and argued in Cyprian's time, but it says nothing of apostolic origin.
It says whose act baptism is, which touches one step of joining but does not describe the process.
It names the old self's distress and ignorance but offers no practice for an unsettled mind.
It tells how the church gave money to ransom captives, not what a person gave up to belong.
It shows Cyprian doubting one letter's authenticity and says nothing of torture or the outside record asked about.
It shows two texts agreeing on the core and differing on one detail, but says nothing of torture or any outside record.
It shows how confessors and the lapsed were dealt with, which bears on how a failed person was regarded but not directly on the asker.
It speaks only of heretics who confess Christ and die outside the Church, not of all outside it, such as those who never heard.
It is Augustine on those who doubt eternal punishment and says nothing of Gregory of Nyssa or the restoration of all things.
It gives the crowd's cry after the sentence in the Acta, which is what was asked.
It states that the believers cried out to be beheaded with him, though it mostly tells the wider death account.
Augustine says his hearers belong to his care so he can give a good account of them, which answers what a pastor owes.
It tells how Cyprian was chosen bishop, which is the story asked for.
Cyprian's own words state the sum sent and where it came from.
It tells the letter, the call to ransom and the sum sent.
It shows the church sending the sum to buy back captives, which is the example asked for.
It tells the whole case of paying to free captives.
It says plague relief reached all people, not only believers, which is the example asked for.
It tells the plague, the sermon on loving enemies and help to everyone.
It tells how Augustine had penance psalms copied and wept over them, which answers the question about a bishop weeping over his sins.
It is Augustine on John 6 and eating the food that lasts, not a reading of John 1:1 'In the beginning was the Word'.
It is a real account of a presbyter's wife and family, but it answers none of the speaker's own childhood, wife or house.
It is about councils correcting earlier councils and scripture's place, not whether a council voted Jesus into being God.
It shows the Lord answering a blow while ready in heart for more, but the record says it takes up no ruling on self-defence.
It shows the church paying to ransom captive members, not care for its own poor and widows.
